title: parallel silently serializes any send steps — the shared shell session has a single-slot execution lock, so the most common use gets zero concurrency
existing_state: ParallelCommand runs each branch via Task.Run against one shared ScriptContext (Services/Scripting/Commands/ParallelCommand.cs:40-61), with a comment at line 45 deferring to 'internal synchronization'. That synchronization is SshShellSession._commandExecutionLock, a SemaphoreSlim(1,1) (Services/SshShellSession.cs:75) acquired by every command-execution path: ExecuteAsync (536-552), the expect variant (573-594), and ExecuteWithRespondsAsync (615-653). So when a user puts send steps in parallel branches — the natural thing to try in an SSH tool — they execute strictly one at a time on the single shell channel. The user gets the threading overhead, the result-ordering complexity, and concurrent StepStarting/StepCompleted events, but no actual speedup; nothing warns them. Concurrency is only real for local/network utility steps (ping, portcheck, webhook, wait, dns).
recommendation: Make the behavior honest at validation time: in ScriptParser validation (or a preflight in ParallelCommand), detect send/interactive steps inside parallel branches and emit a warning ('send steps inside parallel run sequentially on the shared SSH session'), plus a line in the script docs and the Flow Canvas parallel block's property panel. As a follow-up feature (separate, ~a week), real concurrency is achievable: the Rebex connection pool already exists, so parallel branches containing sends could each check out their own pooled channel for the branch duration.
user_benefit: Users stop architecting scripts around a parallelism that does not exist for SSH commands, and understand why their parallel device interrogation takes exactly as long as sequential.

evidence.note: Task.Run per branch over one shared ScriptContext/session; comment at 45 defers to session synchronization
all three command execution paths serialize on the single-slot lock
